title: How to Answer Your Child's Hard Questions About God
excerpt: When your child asks a question you cannot answer, the answer they most need is not certainty. It is a parent who will not flinch and will not lie.
body:
Sooner or later your child will ask you something about God that you cannot answer, and how you respond in that moment will teach them more than the answer ever could. Why did grandma die? If God is real, why is there so much suffering? How do you know the Bible is true? Why does God let bad things happen to kids? These questions are not attacks on the faith. They are the faith, growing up, starting to feel the weight of the world.

The worst thing you can do is panic, shut it down, or fake a certainty you do not have. Children can smell a parent bluffing, and a faith that cannot survive a hard question is a faith they will leave the moment they meet a hard world.

## Welcome the question before you answer it

The first move is not the answer. It is the welcome. "That is a really good question." "I am glad you asked me that." You are teaching your child that doubt and hard questions are allowed in this house, that they can bring their honest confusion to you and to God without being shamed for it.

This matters enormously. Many people who left the faith did not leave over an argument. They left because the question they raised as a teenager was met with anger or fear, and they concluded the whole thing was too fragile to hold their real thoughts. Do not make the faith look brittle by guarding it nervously. A confident faith can sit with a hard question for a long time.

## Say "I don't know" when you don't

You will not have all the answers, and pretending you do is the fastest way to lose your credibility. When you do not know, say so. "I don't know. That is one of the hardest questions there is, and people much smarter than me have wrestled with it for thousands of years."

This does not weaken your witness. It strengthens it. You are showing your child that faith is not the absence of unanswered questions, that you can trust God without understanding everything, that honest is more durable than airtight. "I don't know, but here is what I do believe" is one of the most faith-building sentences a parent can say.

## Sit in the hard ones honestly

For the question of suffering, do not reach for a tidy answer, because there is not one and your child will know it. The Bible itself does not hand us a clean theory of pain. It hands us Job, who never gets his explanation, and a God who shows up in the whirlwind rather than in a syllogism. It hands us Jesus weeping at a tomb he was about to open.

So sit in it with your child. "I don't fully understand why God allows suffering. But I know he is not far from it. Jesus cried at his friend's grave. God came into the suffering himself, on the cross. He did not stay away from the pain." That is not a solved problem. It is a God in the room, which is what a hurting child actually needs.

## Point past yourself

You are not the source of your child's faith, and you cannot argue them into it. Your job is to be honest, to keep the door open, and to point them to God himself. When you do not have the answer, you can still say, "Let's ask God about it together," and pray the question out loud. You can still open the Bible and look together rather than lecturing.

The aim is not to win every conversation but to keep your child in the conversation, with you and with God, for the long haul. A child who learns they can bring anything to God will keep coming back to him long after they stop needing you to translate.

## This week

The next time your child asks something hard about God, do not rush to fix it. Welcome the question first, answer honestly, and if you do not know, say so and turn it into something you wrestle with together. If you want to be ready, the deep guide at /life/raising-children-in-grace sits with several of these questions at length. But readiness is not the point. Being a parent who does not flinch is the point. Let your child learn this week that there is no question too big to bring to you, and none too big to bring to God.
